extracted.intended_audience: researchers and academics aspiring to be peer reviewers for Taylor & Francis journals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for researchers on how to become a peer reviewer for academic journals and how to prepare and write an effective peer review report for Taylor & Francis journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: The peer review process may adopt one of the following forms: Single-blind review (reviewer’s name isn’t disclosed to the author); Double-blind review (identities of reviewers and authors aren’t disclosed); Open review (both author and reviewer names are disclosed); Post-publication open review (readers and reviewers can post comments after publication, mediated by the editor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Single- and double-blind review are the most common methods. Be aware which form the journal uses before agreeing to review and tailor confidentiality/tone accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact editor to become reviewer
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors welcome new reviewers, especially in under-represented areas. Email the editor with areas of expertise, publication record, and interest in reviewing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you regularly read a journal, contacting the editor directly is a practical route to being added to their reviewer pool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask senior colleague for recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask a colleague who knows your work and is involved with the journal to pass on your details to the editor or recommend you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Colleagues may also share helpful advice from their own early reviewing experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look out for calls for reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals (especially new ones or those expanding scope) may invite prospective reviewers to get in touch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responding to explicit calls can be a direct path to joining a journal's reviewer pool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Register with publisher reviewer database
rubrics_metrics.description: Some publishers invite aspiring reviewers to add details to a reviewer database (e.g., specifying research specialisms and journals of interest).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registering increases visibility to editors searching for reviewers with specific expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find a mentor for reviewing
rubrics_metrics.description: Work with a senior colleague experienced in reviewing, or join journal mentoring schemes designed to support first-time reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentoring can involve co-reviewing and provides hands-on guidance on writing reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be visible on researcher networking sites
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain detailed profiles on platforms such as ResearchGate or Academia.edu including research areas and links to publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed profiles make it easier for editors to discover you as a potential reviewer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish to increase reviewer invitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors who publish in a journal often are added to that journal’s database of reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submitting papers or reviews to a journal can lead to future review invitations; however, one should not publish solely to obtain reviewer status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research the journal before reviewing
rubrics_metrics.description: Visit the journal homepage to understand its content, house style, aims and scope, and read the Instructions for Authors (e.g., length, scope, presentation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This helps judge whether the manuscript suits the journal and identify house-style expectations to cite in feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check submission logistics before agreeing
rubrics_metrics.description: Before agreeing, consider the form of review, how you must submit your review (structured form or free text), and whether you can meet the deadline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inform the editor immediately about conflicts of interest or inability to meet the deadline so they can make alternative arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declare conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers must declare any conflict of interest before agreeing to review a manuscript, including any relationship with the author that may bias the review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept a review if a conflict cannot be managed; inform the editor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adhere to ethical guidelines for reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should be aware of and follow ethical guidelines (Taylor & Francis recommends COPE Ethical Guidelines for Peer Reviewers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical adherence includes confidentiality, unbiased evaluation, and appropriate conduct when identifying similarities to other work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain confidentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers must keep the peer review process confidential and not share manuscript information or correspondence outside the process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not discuss or distribute manuscript content; respect blinded identities as required by review form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide constructive, comprehensive, evidenced reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should provide constructive, comprehensive, evidenced, and appropriately substantial peer review reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports should include specific evidence and actionable suggestions; avoid vague statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid impugning reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers must avoid making statements that could be construed as impugning any person’s reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep criticism focused on the work and evidence, not on personal attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be timely and communicate delays
rubrics_metrics.description: Make reasonable effort to submit reports on time, and inform the editor if unable to meet deadlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timeliness helps editorial workflow; if delayed, editors can reassign or inform authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flag significant similarity / possible plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should alert the editor to any significant similarity between the manuscript and published or submitted works of which they are aware.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide references or details to help the editor investigate potential overlap or plagiarism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary evaluation factors: originality, presentation, relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the two main factors reviewers should advise on: the originality, presentation, and relevance of the manuscript’s subject matter to the readership of the journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the paper is original, fits the journal's scope, is of interest to readers, advances the field, and whether significance/impact is high or low.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary evaluation factor: methodological accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: The other main factor reviewers should advise on: the accuracy of the methodology and any analysis provided in the manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that methods are appropriate, applied correctly, and sufficiently described to support conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the submission original? Does it significantly build on the author’s previous work or offer novel contributions?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate novelty against existing literature; indicate where the contribution is incremental versus substantial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit to journal scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the paper fit the scope of the journal?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If out of scope, recommend alternative journals or advise rejection for that journal while noting its value elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest to readership
rubrics_metrics.description: Would the paper be of interest to the readership of the journal?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the journal’s audience and topical priorities when assessing impact and relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contribution to the field
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the paper help to expand or further research in this subject area?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how the findings open new directions, fill gaps, or resolve debates; comment on the strength of the evidence for claimed contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance and potential impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the significance and potential impact of a paper is high or low.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give reasoned judgements on significance, not just assertions; relate impact to audience and field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness (abstract, conclusion, structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the paper complete? Does it include an abstract/summary and a clear conclusion?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag missing structural elements and suggest where summaries or conclusions should be strengthened.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data, citations, and references completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Are all relevant accompanying data, citations, or references provided by the author?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request missing data, supplementary materials, or citations; check that claims are supported by cited evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form/length suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the manuscript need shortening or changing to another form?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If recommending shortening, identify specific areas to cut or condense; suggest alternate article types if appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Key editorial recommendations to give: Accept (suitable as is); Minor revision (ready after light revisions, list revisions); Major revision (needs substantial changes such as expanded analysis or rewriting); Reject (not suitable or revisions too fundamental).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear, itemized revision requests for minor/major cases; after revision, reviewers may be asked to confirm whether revisions are satisfactory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and readability (Standard English)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the submission in Standard English to aid the reader’s understanding?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While not responsible for full English editing, reviewers should point out where language obscures meaning and may suggest professional English editing for non-native speakers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide detailed, author-facing comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments should be suitable for sending to the author: constructive suggestions, requests for clarification, and prompts for further elaboration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor feedback to the paper, avoid vague or generalised statements, and ensure comments make clear what actions authors should take.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and wording: be critical but sensitive
rubrics_metrics.description: Be critical whilst remaining sensitive to the author; word comments carefully so authors understand required actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include positive feedback as well as constructive criticism; avoid irrelevant negative remarks and abrasive language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct English only where technical meaning unclear
rubrics_metrics.description: It is helpful to correct English where the technical meaning is unclear, but it is not the reviewer’s job to edit the paper fully for English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out problematic sentences and, where helpful, offer suggested rephrasings, especially when they affect interpretation of results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow unsupported opinions to stand if evidence supports them
rubrics_metrics.description: A referee may disagree with the author’s opinions, but should allow them to stand, provided their evidence supports it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus challenges on evidence and reasoning rather than forcing conformity of viewpoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use sample comment templates
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of positive, constructive, and linguistic comments are provided as templates for phrasing feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples (e.g., 'The manuscript is well written', 'This paper would benefit from…', 'To make this paper publishable, the author needs to respond to the following substantive points…') as a model but tailor to the manuscript.
